TOKYO, Oct 27 : Moody's sees encouraging signs in Japan's return to sustained growth and stable inflation, but a key test will be whether that resilience can withstand future shocks, the rating agency's Japan sovereign analyst told Reuters on Tuesday. Moody's rates Japan at A1, its fifth-highest investment-grade rating, with a stable outlook, unchanged since its 2014 downgrade of Japan from Aa3. "We're starting to see what looks more like sustained growth and inflation expectations that are reasonably well anchored around 2 per cent," said Martin Petch, a vice president at the sovereign risk group of Moody's Ratings. "That's been something that's changed," Petch said in an interview, referring to a shift from decades of weak growth and chronically low inflation.

Petch declined to speculate on future rating actions, but said Moody's was watching to see if recent changes in Japan's economic and inflation environment prove sustainable, along with reforms that boost productivity and tackle demographic woes. A key test, he added, is whether Japan can maintain growth and inflation stability through future economic shocks. "You can generally tell when growth has become sustained when the economy has dealt with a shock," Petch said, pointing out that Japan had coped well with recent energy-price shocks while the central bank keeps up efforts to normalise policy. LITTLE IMMEDIATE THREAT SEEN TO CREDIT PROFILE Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's food sales tax cut and ambitious spending plans rattled bond markets this year, but Petch suggested the measures have posed little immediate threat to Japan's credit profile. Their fiscal impact would depend on whether the government delivered on its pledge to offset the resulting revenue loss, he added. Although ministries have sought a record 143 trillion yen ($908 billion) in initial spending requests, Petch said the rise was relatively modest compared with combined initial and supplementary budgets. This reinforced Moody's view that there has been no meaningful departure from Japan's recent consolidation trend, he added. But uncertainties hover over the government's 370-trillion-yen public-private investment initiative, Petch said. These include the extent to which the private sector joins the initiative, and whether it can bring the productivity gains needed to offset Japan's demographic headwinds, he added. ($1=157.4700 yen)

Source: Reuters

SEOUL, Oct 27 : South Korea's semiconductor exports could fall by $50 billion to $100 billion compared with earlier forecasts if capital spending on artificial intelligence by major US technology firms slows next year, according to central bank data. In a written response submitted to lawmaker Ahn Do-geol, the Bank of Korea (BOK) modelled a "pessimistic scenario" to assess the economic fallout if US tech giants curb their aggressive infrastructure outlays. Under the scenario, a sudden export shortfall would shave approximately 0.4 per centage point off South Korea's gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate next year, by driving the country's current account surplus well below the central bank's initial projection of $430 billion for 2027. The scenario assumed a 10 per cent decline in Korean semiconductor unit prices.

The report said combined capital expenditure by five major US technology firms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle, has been growing rapidly, from $40 billion last year to an estimated $80 billion this year, and is projected to reach $110 billion next year. However, the BOK cautioned that considerable uncertainty remains over the trajectory of AI demand and the broader memory chip business cycle.

SEOUL, Oct 27 : South Korean pop music agency JYP Entertainment's shares jumped 10 per cent on Tuesday after Korean media reported Japan's Nexroc Group and related firm SVCV Inc were planning to announce a tender offer to buy up to a 50 per cent stake in the company. The 50 per cent stake is worth about 700 billion won ($528.04 million) based on JYP's current market capitalisation. JYP said it has not received a tender offer. Nexroc Group was not immediately available to comment. JYP Entertainment, founded by South Korean singer-songwriter and producer Park Jin-young (J.Y. Park), is one of South Korea’s leading K-pop entertainment companies, with its main artists including popular K-pop groups such as TWICE, Stray Kids, ITZY and DAY6.

The two companies said in a press release that they are targeting between 25 per cent and 50 per cent of JYP's issued shares, with a tender offer price at a 30 per cent premium to a benchmark share price, Yonhap News Agency and other media said. "The 'pre-tender offer announcement' of JYP Entertainment by NEXROC and SVCV is not typical and could be made illegal by the Korean financial authorities," said Douglas Kim, an independent analyst who writes on Smartkarma. "A company has to launch a tender offer when they have enough financial backing/assets that would allow them to launch a tender offer," he said, adding that allowing such a pre-tender offer "could set a bad precedent in the Korean equity markets." Oct 27 : Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday as the potential for a resolution in the US-Israeli war on Iran kept supply fears at bay, but Brent stayed close to six-month highs as attacks on Saudi Arabia lowered hopes of immediate stability in the region. Brent crude futures were down 66 cents, or 0.57 per cent, at $115.15 a barrel as of 0000 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude was down 44 cents, or 0.43 per cent, at $101.32. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday aimed at easing tensions in the Middle East. Saudi Arabia said the visit sought to establish open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation". The four countries agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation in peace and security, Iranian state media reported. Hopes of resolution in the conflict erased some fears of supply disruption, lowering risks and pressuring oil prices.

October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. The war has rippled across the Middle East, placing the Strait of Hormuz at the center of the turmoil. The narrow waterway carried around a fifth of the world's energy supplies before the conflict erupted in February. Last week, Brent prices surged to more than $117 a barrel, the highest level since April, after a wave of Iranian attacks on tankers around the strait. Brent prices touched $117 on Monday as well. Elsewhere, Russian refiners are raising diesel production in October after the government granted export quotas following the Kremlin's supply agreement with the US, two industry sources close to the matter said.

MADRID, Oct 26 : Spain on Monday unveiled a more flexible version of its proposed decree governing data centers after a wave of project announcements in the country, according to officials at the energy ministry. • The revised proposal raises the threshold for the rules to apply, extends the time frame for developers to demonstrate renewable-energy commitments and introduces a transition period for meeting clean-power targets. • The initial proposal said that rules would apply to facilities with more than 1 megawatt of power capacity. That threshold has now been increased to more than 10 MW. • Originally, every new megawatt of energy used had to be matched by a new megawatt of renewable energy installed in the 18 months before the facility starts operation. Now, the time frame has been extended to 36 months before the start of operation, and there is no time limit for solar energy.

Oct 26 : Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley will provide $63 billion in financing to buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic, in one of the largest debt deals tied to the AI buildout. Broadcom is providing "residual value support" to lenders, who are providing first lien loans or senior debt, effectively providing a significant guarantee in the financing structure. The latest deal highlights the growing role of banks and alternative asset managers in financing the infrastructure needed to support rising demand for AI computing capacity. Anthropic filed for a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, even as disclosures of steep losses and security concerns threatened to test investor appetite for the AI heavyweight.

The size of the first lien loans or senior debt is about $43.5 billion, according to two sources familiar with the matter, or 69 per cent of total financing. Blackstone will provide the committed portion of the second-lien financing - which ranks below senior debt - while Bank of America, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley are arranging the first-lien financing, the statement said. Chipmakers have provided guarantees in the past to absorb potential declines in the value of the assets, such as advanced chips and data infrastructure. The release did not disclose the breakdown of the loans, while Broadcom did not respond to a request for comment. Rising AI demand is driving massive investment in computing infrastructure as technology companies race to secure capacity for increasingly complex workloads. The transaction will be carried out through a newly formed special purpose vehicle that will purchase Broadcom's AI accelerators and networking equipment and lease them to the Claude maker, the companies said on Monday. Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley are arranging the first-lien financing.  Deliveries are expected to begin in 2027 as part of a previously announced strategic compute capacity agreement involving Broadcom, the companies said. Apollo and Blackstone had agreed to finance a $35 billion expansion of Anthropic's AI computing capacity under a prior agreement with Broadcom. Broadcom's backstop in that deal was up to $29 billion, it said in a filing. While Moody's described Broadcom as one of the strongest large technology companies, it warned that the risk would increase if multiple transactions were undertaken over a short period to meet the sizable funding needs of frontier AI labs.

Source: Reuters

Oct 26 : Canadian AI company Cohere said on Monday one of Alibaba's Qwen AI models tried to send data to an Alibaba Cloud storage server in Beijing during a security test. The model made the attempt even though its own reasoning indicated it would not do such a thing, Cohere said. Alibaba was not immediately available for comment outside regular business hours. • Cohere, which sells its own AI models to businesses and governments as a "sovereign AI" provider, competes with open-weight models such as Alibaba's Qwen, which anyone can download and run on their own servers • Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next was asked to write a rule to detect malicious file download, but instead took stock of the machine it was running on and tried to send a test file to the Beijing server, Cohere said

NEW YORK: US stocks closed higher on Monday (Oct 26), with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq coming off consecutive weekly declines, as Anthropic's IPO filing helped boost sentiment in AI-related stocks in a week filled with a host of market catalysts. Anthropic disclosed steep losses and red-hot revenue growth in its filing for a US initial public offering, laying out its ambition to build AI systems capable of reshaping the global economy despite the high costs of developing the technology. The AI lab is pushing ahead with its listing plans even as a once-lively autumn IPO calendar has slowed, with recent market volatility prompting companies to delay offerings. Anthropic's filing comes as investors increasingly dissect the potential payoff from massive AI spending and at the start of an eventful week. On tap are the Federal Reserve's policy statement on Wednesday, readings on economic growth and inflation on Thursday and a slew of corporate earnings reports throughout the week.

More than a third of S&P 500 companies are scheduled to report earnings this week, including hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon.com, whose results will be parsed for signs of whether the hefty AI investments are translating into growth. "Today's all about the Anthropic release, so we're back on a little bit of an optimistic tilt, I would say. But there's a lot in that release. It will be interesting to see how well things are received when they actually come to list," said JP Powers, chief investment officer at RWA Wealth Partners in Boston. "The risk is maybe a little bit of a whipsaw if things aren't all moving in the same direction. A little optimism today, but who knows what will happen from some of these other releases this week," he said. According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 gained 53.35 points, or 0.70 per cent, to end at 7,677.03 points, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 214.02 points, or 0.83 per cent, to 26,169.38. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 146.60 points, or 0.28 per cent, to 52,361.76. Semiconductor and chip-related companies, widely viewed as some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, helped fuel the gains. The broader Philadelphia chips index was up about 3 per cent on the day but is still down nearly 12 per cent on the month.

Meta said on Monday it plans to raise up to US$95 billion in equity to fund its AI-related expansion of data centers, cloud computing power and other infrastructure. The AI trade has come under pressure this month amid concerns that debt-funded spending may become harder to justify in the face of climbing borrowing costs. The Anthropic filing helped buoy sentiment, however, as neocloud firms, including CoreWeave, erased earlier declines. Other AI-linked companies, including photonic product makers Lumentum and Coherent, were among the best-performing S&P 500 stocks. The technology index led gains among the 11 major S&P 500 sectors. Megacap and growth stocks were also mostly higher. Tesla jumped to its highest intraday level in more than three months after Barclays upgraded its rating on the stock to "overweight" from "equal-weight". Markets are pricing in only a 12.7 per cent chance of a rate hike from the Fed on Wednesday, according to CME FedWatch. But with inflation pressures showing no signs of abating, market participants do not believe the central bank will be on hold for long. Investors are also bracing for the Nov 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the US Congress.

Oct 26 : Anthropic paused training of its next-generation flagship AI model for more than a month over security concerns, while four of its AI agents accessed live external computer systems during testing, its initial public offering filing showed on Monday. The Claude maker said in the filing's risk factors section that it had delayed pre-training of a new "frontier" base model to strengthen safeguards against the theft of model weights and intellectual property. The disclosure highlights the safety challenges facing developers of increasingly powerful AI models, some of whose creators have warned the technology could eventually escape human control. Rival OpenAI also paused some training earlier this year over safety concerns after its models hacked Hugging Face. The incidents illustrate how unexpected safety failures could disrupt development and deployment of models central to Anthropic's growth as it prepares for a widely anticipated stock market debut.

Anthropic warned that training pauses could delay revenue and leave it trailing competitors. The company devoted about 94 pages to risk factors, more than in its confidential filing seen by Reuters. SANDBOX ESCAPE The filing also detailed previously undisclosed safety evaluation failures in which four AI models escaped their testing environments and accessed real-world computer systems, with sessions lasting between 10 and 34 hours. Anthropic said an error during cybersecurity tests with a third-party partner left the testing environment connected to the internet despite instructions that web access be disabled. In one instance, an early version of the model continued pursuing an impossible evaluation task, discovered a stored password and used it to gain administrator access to a third party's system. It then obtained additional credentials, changed system settings and accessed an individual's personal data. The filing did not identify the external parties involved. Anthropic said it notified all affected parties and found no evidence that the models had sought to evade human oversight or coordinate with each other. It subsequently suspended certain pre-release cybersecurity evaluations and paused higher-risk reinforcement learning environments. Separately, the company said on Sunday that Claude had bypassed a paywall and accessed publicly available aggregate voter counts from the US state of Georgia without human authorization.

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 26 : Unconventional AI, the US hardware startup that launched less than a year ago with a $4.5 billion valuation, said on Monday that it is buying Israeli chip startup NeuReality for an undisclosed sum in a cash-and-stock deal. Unconventional AI raised $475 million in December and is led by Naveen Rao, who previously sold chip startup Nervana to Intel for more than $400 million and AI software startup MosaicML to Databricks for $1.3 billion. It is backed by prominent Silicon Valley venture firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia, along with Amazon.com founder Jeff Bezos, among others. Mountain View, California-based Unconventional AI's goal is to develop AI chips that are 1,000 times more energy efficient than current offerings by using concepts from biological systems. The company is focusing on what Rao calls a "dynamical systems" approach, in which simple computing elements interact with simple rules and evolve over time to reach a result, rather than following programmed step-by-step logic as conventional computing chips do. In an interview, Rao said that when Unconventional AI raised its $475 million war chest of cash, the company expected to take three years in research and development and take five years to develop a product.

Oct 26 : Anthropic unveiled its US initial public offering paperwork on Monday, setting up for a blockbuster market debut that would test investors' willingness to fund the AI juggernaut's bills amid growing worries over the massive debt-fueled spending. The company had submitted a confidential filing in June. In the recent weeks, exclusive reporting from Reuters highlighted its sweeping AI ambitions, mounting costs and concerns about the "existential risks to humanity" that advanced AI poses. Here are a few details on Anthropic's financials, business structure, and where it stands in the global AI race: BACKGROUND AND FINANCES

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic is the startup behind the Claude family of AI models. Across four tiers - Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku - Claude powers products such as Anthropic's chatbot, coding agent and the enterprise-focused Claude Cowork AI agent. Anthropic's early focus on training its models for coding tasks propelled the company to the forefront of the AI race and helped it draw a steady stream of enterprise customers. A majority of its revenue comes from businesses paying for its models per use, measured in "tokens" of information processed, in what Anthropic calls "consumption-based" revenue. It also generates revenue from its paid customer subscription tiers such as "Pro" and "Max". That has helped Anthropic grow its revenue to $4.59 billion in 2025 from $386 million a year ago and $41 million in 2023. For the six months ended June 2026, Anthropic's revenue was $16.29 billion, a massive increase from $1.16 billion for the same period in 2025. The company's operating losses have ballooned over the past years. But for the first half of 2026, they stood at $693 million, narrowing from $2.14 billion in the first half of 2025, as a fourteen-fold jump in revenue offset a fivefold increase in overall expenses. COSTS, COMPUTE DEMAND AND CIRCULAR AI INVESTMENTS Computing power is Anthropic's biggest expense. The company's costs include computing fees paid to cloud services providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, costs tied to data center facilities and renting data center capacity, equipment leases and energy bills. Over the past three years, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure expenses have dwarfed its revenue. The company has committed more than $600 billion in spending with about eight partners over a decade - one of the largest AI buildout commitments on record. Anthropic said many portions of its agreements are non-cancelable or require payments regardless of usage. It has committed to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon, about $114.5 billion with Google and $44.9 billion with Microsoft for cloud computing over the next seven to 10 years. But some of those companies are also its largest backers. Amazon and Google are among Anthropic's top shareholders, marking yet another example of the circular financing structures that have dominated capital flows in the AI industry. Amazon has invested at least $13 billion in Anthropic and has agreed to invest up to $20 billion more. Google has committed up to $40 billion to Anthropic. GOVERNANCE AND STRUCTURE Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, or PBC, meaning it is legally obligated to balance profitability goals for investors with developing AI for the benefit of humanity. An independent body elects a majority of its board. The company, helmed by Dario Amodei as CEO and his sister Daniela, as president and chair of the board, will continue to operate as a PBC after its listing. It expects to keep its founders and an independent trust in control, in a structure that could limit investor oversight and public shareholders' influence. The company has said it needs to concentrate control and capital in fewer hands to reduce AI's risks. Under this arrangement, a majority vote of its seven co-founders will direct a single share of Class F stock that amounts to 50.1 per cent of the total voting power over key corporate matters, including the election of some board directors and other matters submitted to investors. COMPETITION Anthropic's most direct competitor is OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, whose 2022 launch kick-started the global race to adopt and advance AI technologies. Following Anthropic's lead in the enterprise market, OpenAI has sharpened its focus on products for developers and business customers. Anthropic is also locked in a race with Elon Musk's SpaceX, Alphabet's Google and Meta. All of them are spending billions of dollars into model development, data centers and specialized AI chips as they vie for dominance in generative AI. Ramp data, which captures a slice of AI spending by business customers, showed Anthropic accounted for 60.1 per cent of AI token spending in the week ended October 11.

Source: Reuters

Oct 26 : Anthropic took a big step closer to a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, even as it revealed steep losses and security concerns that could test investors' enthusiasm for the AI heavyweight. AI has captured investors' imagination with the promise of a technological leap that could transform businesses, accelerate scientific breakthroughs and unlock vast productivity gains. That has fueled enormous investments in computing infrastructure and AI development, while also stoking skepticism over the scale and pace of the spending. Anthropic's listing comes at a critical time for global markets as investors closely assess whether the billions of dollars being poured into the technology will generate returns to justify sky-high valuations.

"There is still enormous excitement about AI's potential to transform businesses, turbocharge productivity and reshape entire industries, but investors are becoming more discerning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club. Anthropic's net loss in the first half of 2026 widened sharply to $80.7 billion, largely due to a non-operating item related to bonds convertible into the company's shares. Despite the huge expenses, its operating loss for the same period narrowed to $693 million and its adjusted operating income swung to a positive $1.62 billion compared with a loss of $1.85 billion a year ago. The company, which is expected to go public before Thanksgiving, said its revenue grew a staggering 1,368 per cent in the three months ended June 30 from a year ago, but it warned in the prospectus that its revenue growth rate could decline and fluctuate from time to time. The filing confirmed a series of Reuters exclusives that offered an early peek at its contents before Anthropic made it public, including details of its financial performance, growth trajectory and IPO plans. Its prospectus details the risks from the powerful technology, from potential misuse and security threats to concerns that advanced systems could produce outputs that "could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative", including behavior resembling blackmail. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown in the development of AI. VALUATION EXPECTATIONS Some current and prospective investors are valuing Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion a week ago, after the AI startup disclosed some financial details at a recent investor event. "The offering is for the faithful, that sooner or later, they're going to get some return on that invested capital," said Thomas Hayes, chairman at Great Hill Capital. Anthropic's IPO currently stands alone in what was once expected to be a crowded fall listing market. Analysts said that would give it access to a deep pool of capital to fund its costly AI ambitions. "Anthropic's IPO will establish a benchmark for valuing leading AI labs, influencing both upcoming listings and confidence in the companies funding the AI infrastructure build-out," IPOX research associate Lukas Muehlbauer said. Analysts expect valuations of the AI sector to correct as investor unease with the debt-fueled AI investment boom roils equity and debt markets. Higher borrowing costs and rising bond yields have also added to investor caution. "Anthropic is entering an IPO market that is far more challenging than the summer. Investors were not questioning valuations the same way a few months ago," said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, a provider of IPO-focused research and ETFs. BALANCING AI'S PROMISES AND PERILS Anthropic said more than half of Fortune 500 companies and over 30 per cent of Global 2000 firms were its customers that generated at least $100,000 each in revenue for the company over the 12 months ended September 30. The IPO comes as Anthropic's own research raises concerns about advanced AI systems, which in controlled tests have shown behaviors including code sabotage, fraud assistance and information manipulation. "Our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures," the prospectus said. The company said it relies on a limited number of cloud services providers such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft and suppliers such as Broadcom for compute and critical infrastructure parts. These relationships can create "dependencies and potential vulnerabilities", it said. Anthropic, which did not reveal the terms of its offering, will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" after the IPO closes. SCORCHING PACE OF GROWTH Anthropic, founded in 2021 by a team of researchers who left OpenAI after disagreements over governance and AI safety, was valued at $965 billion in a funding round in May. It remains locked in a fierce battle with OpenAI to lead the race to build the most advanced AI systems. The company named Netflix's billionaire co-founder Reed Hastings as its lead independent director. In keeping with Nasdaq rules, Anthropic identified itself as a "controlled company" based on the power of its Long-Term Benefit Trust to elect a majority of its board. The company said it expects compute and infrastructure expenses to rise in absolute dollars and remain its largest operating expense. Anthropic has committed more than $600 billion to computing deals with partners including Amazon and Google, ranking among the largest AI infrastructure commitments on record. Anthropic's IPO follows that of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which rewrote the IPO record books in June, when it priced a $75 billion offering that valued the company at $1.75 trillion. Goldman Sachs secured the prestigious lead-left role on Anthropic's IPO, working alongside Morgan Stanley, which is also a lead underwriter. Both banks declined to comment. Twenty other banks were named as underwriters with Morgan Stanley serving as stabilization agent, overseeing the stock's early trading. The IPO mandates mark another win for the two banks, which also held lead roles in SpaceX's IPO.

Source: Reuters

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 26 : Cadence Design Systems on Monday launched a portfolio of AI models tuned to help design computer chips, deepening its open-source model work with Nvidia and diverging from rival Synopsys' recent deal with OpenAI. Both companies make software used to design computing chips — a process that involves arranging billions of transistors precisely to meet cost and performance targets — and are racing to have AI "agents" use those tools on behalf of human engineers to speed up the process. The new suite, called Cadence Maestro, introduced on Monday, was built in part on Nvidia's open-weight Nemotron model and secured with Nvidia's OpenShell safety technology, the companies said. Cadence said customers can run the models on its own cloud or any public cloud, or keep them entirely in-house behind their own firewalls and data centers.

Shares of Cadence, which reports earnings after market close on Monday, rose 3.9 per cent after the announcement. Customers can also fine-tune the models on their own chip designs, and early results show up to 30 per cent higher quality and up to five times better cost-efficiency than general-purpose models, it added. The Cadence approach contrasts with that of its largest competitor, Synopsys, which on September 30 said it would develop an AI model with OpenAI and share revenue with the ChatGPT maker. That model, GPT-Synopsys, will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure. Paul Cunningham, a Cadence senior vice president, framed Maestro as model-agnostic, saying, "there are more (AI) model providers out there than there are (chip design software) vendors." When asked whether Cadence might strike its own deals with proprietary AI labs, Cunningham said both open- and closed-weight approaches were being "pursued equally," and that working with commercial labs was "part of the Maestro vision," though he declined to elaborate. The first Maestro models will reach select early-access customers in the fourth quarter, Cadence said.

Oct 26 : T-Mobile on Monday unveiled wireless plans that let customers pick and swap perks from Netflix to DoorDash, moving away from its traditional strategy of locking benefits into fixed plan tiers.  The move mirrors customizable offerings from rivals such as Verizon, but T-Mobile's new plans include selected streaming, music and other subscriptions at no extra cost beyond the monthly plan price.  • T-Mobile is betting that offering greater control over benefits will attract customers spending on multiple subscriptions, as competition among US carriers moves beyond network coverage and smartphone promotions • Netflix was the most popular benefit in a pilot launched in early October, T-Mobile Chief Marketing Officer Allan Samson told Reuters in an interview
